idiom_name: java.util.concurrent CyclicBarrier / CountDownLatch on the JVM
implementation_notes: On the JVM, Scala's most direct realization is the same java.util.concurrent machinery Java uses: CyclicBarrier(n) for a reusable phase rendezvous (with an optional action run by the last arriver), CountDownLatch for one-shot fan-in, Phaser when parties register and deregister between phases. Scala's sugar is thin here - the primitives are called as in Java, typically from dedicated pools or computation threads - and this is the only variant that covers the reusable barrier, because the Future API expresses completion, not rendezvous.
pitfalls: Scala.js and Scala Native have no java.util.concurrent at all, so the JVM primitives simply do not exist there - the Future-based variant is the portable one, and it has no reusable barrier.
await() inside a Future body blocks an execution-context thread and can starve the EC; keep barriers on dedicated threads or pools the EC does not own.

InterruptedException and BrokenBarrierException are checked at the JVM level and surface as non-local behaviours in Scala; convert them into the domain's failure type explicitly instead of letting a bare try/catch swallow the break.

variants.name: scala.concurrent futures as the fan-in
variants.idiom_name: Future.sequence + onComplete/andThen, Await only at the boundary
variants.implementation_notes: The latch's meaning - proceed once N computations have finished - is expressed functionally as Future.sequence(futures) followed by a continuation: registering onComplete or andThen never blocks a thread, and failures short-circuit the combined future so the collector is a pure function of the outcomes. Await.result remains for the boundary where a result is unavoidable, and this is the portable form (Scala.js/Native). What the functional style cannot express is a reusable phase barrier: rendezvous still requires the blocking primitives or a channel/actor-based protocol.
variants.code_sketch:
import scala.concurrent.{Await, Future}
import scala.concurrent.duration.*
import scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext.Implicits.global

val all: Future[List[Result]] = Future.sequence(shards.map(process))  // latch semantics
val merged: Future[Summary] = all.map(merge)                           // non-blocking
val summary = Await.result(merged, 30.seconds)   // blocking only at the boundary
pitfalls: Await.result blocks a thread and must never run inside the execution context; calling it from a Future deadlocks once the EC's threads are exhausted.
Future.sequence fails fast on the first failure but does not cancel the siblings: the successful futures keep running, so the fan-in is not all-or-nothing unless the work is cancellable.
scala.concurrent has no barrier or latch type, and sharing a mutable counter across Futures is a data race: real rendezvous needs the blocking primitives or an actor/queue protocol.
